1a.html:
Austenite nucleates on interfaces, where carbon is close and the lattice disordered, so the sites follow the starting structure:

  • Pearlite: first at intersections of pearlite colonies, then on ferrite/cementite lamellae. The carbon path is one lamellar spacing, so nuclei are many and several austenite grains form from one colony.
  • Hypoeutectoid (ferrite + pearlite): pearlite transforms first above \mathrm{Ac_1}; proeutectoid ferrite is consumed later, up to \mathrm{Ac_3}, as austenite grows into it with carbon diffusing from the pearlite.
  • Spheroidised: on the carbide particles, mainly those on ferrite boundaries; few large carbides give few nuclei.
  • Ferritic (very low C): at ferrite grain boundaries, especially triple junctions.

Prehistory: finer prior structures (normalised fine pearlite, fine tempered carbides, cold-worked ferrite) give more interface, hence more nuclei; coarse annealed structures give fewer.

Alloy content: carbide formers (Cr, Mo, V) dissolve slowly and raise \mathrm{Ac_1}, delaying nucleation; Mn and Ni lower it. Undissolved V, Nb, Ti or Al carbonitrides pin the new boundaries.

Finest austenite grain: fine, fully pearlitic (or finely dispersed carbide) structure, heated rapidly just above the critical temperature and held only to homogenise, ideally with pinning particles. Coarse ferrite gives the coarsest.
pts: Pearlite: nucleation at colony intersections and on ferrite/cementite lamellae; several austenite grains per colony because diffusion distances are short

1b.html:
Cryotreatment: more than removing retained austenite

Cold treatment (-70 to -120^\circ\mathrm{C}) only completes the austenite-to-martensite change. Deep cryotreatment (-135^\circ\mathrm{C} and below, liquid \mathrm{N_2} at -196^\circ\mathrm{C}, 24 h) also changes the martensite:

  1. The deep chill contracts and strains the lattice, creating defect sites; on the following temper these nucleate a fine, uniform dispersion of coherent transition carbides. The carbide count rises with colder, longer soaks (D2: about 32,000 per \mathrm{mm^2} at +20^\circ\mathrm{C}, 38,000 at -180^\circ\mathrm{C}).
  2. Fine carbides raise wear resistance (tool life 2 to 5 times, wear ratios up to 82) while keeping toughness.
  3. No austenite is left to transform in service: dimensional stability, and one temper is enough.
  4. Chemical: a uniform tempered martensite with fine carbides has fewer micro-galvanic couples (no austenite/martensite pairs, no coarse carbides) and lower residual stress, so corrosion and stress-corrosion resistance improve.

Shrink fit and schedule

Given: AISI 1065 (assumed 0.65% C, 0.75% Mn, 0.25% Si), shaft 200 mm, bore 198 mm, \alpha = 11\times10^{-6}\ ^\circ\mathrm{C^{-1}}.

Step 1. Chill needed (\Delta D = \alpha D \Delta T):

\Delta T = \frac{200 - 198}{(11\times10^{-6})(200)} = 909^\circ\mathrm{C} \;\Rightarrow\; T = 20 - 909 = -889^\circ\mathrm{C}

This is below absolute zero. Liquid nitrogen shrinks the shaft only 11\times10^{-6}(200)(216) = 0.48 mm, and the gear would then need about 720^\circ\mathrm{C} more, which would destroy its hardening. A 1% interference would also overstress the hub. The bore is therefore taken as 199.80 mm (0.1% interference, a heavy shrink fit), plus 0.05 mm assembly clearance:

\Delta T = \frac{0.20 + 0.05}{(11\times10^{-6})(200)} = 114^\circ\mathrm{C} \;\Rightarrow\; T \approx -94^\circ\mathrm{C}, \text{ use } -100^\circ\mathrm{C}

inside the -70 to -120^\circ\mathrm{C} shrink-fitting range.

Step 2. Hardening temperature: A_3 = 910 - 203\sqrt{0.65} + 44.7(0.25) \approx 758^\circ\mathrm{C}, so harden from about 800^\circ\mathrm{C}.

Step 3. Schedule:

  1. \mathrm{CE} = 0.65 + 0.75/5 + (0.25-0.5)/5 = 0.75 \geq 0.7: very crack sensitive; preheat at 600 to 650^\circ\mathrm{C}, heat slowly through 250 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  2. Austenitise at 800^\circ\mathrm{C}, soak 60 + D = 260 min, protective atmosphere.
  3. Quench in agitated oil or polymer. M_s = 520 - 320(0.65) - 50(0.75) \approx 275^\circ\mathrm{C}; M_f \approx -30^\circ\mathrm{C}, so a few % austenite is retained.
  4. Within about 30 min, cold treat at -100^\circ\mathrm{C}, 1 h per 3 cm (about 7 h), then warm to room temperature.
  5. Temper at once, for example 400^\circ\mathrm{C}, about 1 h per 25 mm; finish-grind the seat.
  6. Fit: chill the shaft to -100^\circ\mathrm{C} until cold throughout, insert into the gear at room temperature, let it warm in air.

The cold treatment must precede tempering. If the fitting chill were the first sub-zero step, retained austenite would turn into fresh, untempered, expanded martensite inside the assembled joint.

Answer: harden from about 800^\circ\mathrm{C}; sub-zero at about -100^\circ\mathrm{C} (cold treatment before tempering, and the fitting chill). The printed 2 mm interference cannot be achieved thermally.

2a.html:
The cracking is copper hot shortness: a network of fine surface cracks that opens on forging steel with more than about 0.2% Cu. The most important remedy is adding Ni, about one-third to one-half of the Cu content (up to an equal amount).

Why it cracks

  1. On reheating in an oxidising furnace (1100 to 1250^\circ\mathrm{C}) iron oxidises selectively to scale; Cu, nobler than Fe, is left at the scale/steel interface.
  2. Cu has only limited solubility in austenite, so the enriched interface becomes supersaturated and a Cu-rich phase separates.
  3. Above about 1090^\circ\mathrm{C} this phase is liquid; it wets and penetrates the austenite grain boundaries.
  4. Forging stresses pull these boundaries apart. The effect grows with Cu and C content and with longer, hotter reheating.

How Ni cures it

  • Ni, also nobler than Fe, enriches at the interface with the Cu. Cu and Ni are completely mutually soluble, and Ni raises the melting point of the enriched phase from 1085^\circ\mathrm{C} towards 1455^\circ\mathrm{C}, so it stays solid at forging temperature.
  • Ni raises the solubility of Cu in austenite (synergistic Fe-Cu-Ni system), so less Cu-rich phase separates.
  • The allowable forging temperature rises, up to about 1280^\circ\mathrm{C}, where a protective glaze forms.

Other remedies are impractical: a protective atmosphere is expensive, and hot working below 1090^\circ\mathrm{C} rules out TMT and TMCP rolling.

2b.html:
Molybdenum (MP 2610^\circ\mathrm{C}) is a strong carbide former and a ferrite stabiliser; each property below follows from that.

(i) Hardenability

Dissolved Mo slows the diffusional austenite to ferrite and pearlite reactions: Mo must partition between ferrite and carbide, it diffuses slowly as a large substitutional atom, and it drags the moving \gamma/\alpha interface. The ferrite-pearlite C-curve moves far to the right, the bainite curve less, so a bay opens and thick sections harden in oil or form bainite on air cooling. Grossmann factor f_{\mathrm{Mo}} \approx 1 + 3.0\,\%\mathrm{Mo} (0.2% Mo gives 1.6), so 4140 hardens far deeper than 5140 on the Jominy bar. Mo must be dissolved during austenitising.

(ii) Pitting resistance in chlorides

\mathrm{Cl^-} breaks the Cr-rich passive film locally; the small pit (anode) on a large passive surface becomes acidic and grows autocatalytically. Mo enriches in the passive film as Mo oxide and molybdate, which makes the film more stable against \mathrm{Cl^-} and speeds repassivation. Pitting resistance equivalent \mathrm{PREN} = \%\mathrm{Cr} + 3.3\,\%\mathrm{Mo} + 16\,\%\mathrm{N}: 304 about 18, 316L (2.5% Mo) about 25. Hence 316L instead of 304 in chemical plants and marine service.

(iii) Elevated-temperature strength

Mo strengthens ferrite in solid solution even when hot: large, slow-diffusing atoms resist dislocation climb and creep. It also forms fine, stable \mathrm{Mo_2C} that resists coarsening and softening, and raises the tempering resistance. Hence 0.5Mo, 1Cr-0.5Mo and 2.25Cr-1Mo boiler, pressure-vessel and heat-exchanger steels, which also resist hydrogen attack.

(iv) Wear resistance of tool steels

Mo forms hard \mathrm{M_2C} (about 2000 HV) and \mathrm{M_6C} (about 1500 HV), far harder than martensite (about 800 HV) and \mathrm{Fe_3C}; undissolved carbides resist abrasion. Dissolved Mo re-precipitates as fine \mathrm{Mo_2C} on tempering at 500 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C} (secondary hardening), so the edge stays hard at red heat. M2 high-speed steel (5Mo-6W-2V-4Cr) reaches 64 to 66 HRC after triple tempering at about 550^\circ\mathrm{C}; 1% Mo does the work of about 1.9% W at lower cost.

Common target. Both are subcritical anneals (below \mathrm{A_1}, no phase change) that release stored energy, cold-work strain or residual stress, so the product can be worked further or used safely. The situations that decide how each is done are different:

Process annealingStress-relief annealing
Wherebetween cold-rolling or drawing passes of thin low-C sheet, strip and wirelarge castings, weldments, machined, cold-formed or case-hardened parts
Problemwork hardening has used up ductilityresidual stress from plastic deformation, uneven cooling or phase change
Aimrestore ductility for the next reduction, fine grainremove stress without changing structure or hardness; avoid distortion and SCC
Mechanismrecrystallisation: new strain-free grainsrecovery only: dislocations rearrange
Cycleabout 550 to 650^\circ\mathrm{C}, short hold, non-oxidising atmosphere for thin strip150 to 200^\circ\mathrm{C} after hardening; about 550 to 650^\circ\mathrm{C} after welding or casting; slow heating and cooling
Resulthardness falls sharply, elongation risesproperties almost unchanged

Process annealing is governed by the degree of cold work, the final grain size, surface oxidation and line cost. Stress relief is governed by section size and shape, prior hardness, which must not be lost, dimensional tolerance and the service environment. Cold-worked austenitic stainless steel is stress relieved below 480^\circ\mathrm{C} or above 900^\circ\mathrm{C} to avoid sensitisation.

Method. After quenching, the structure is martensite plus retained austenite (RA), so the martensite fraction is M = 100 - \mathrm{RA}. The printed relation gives the hardness expected for 0.70% C at that M; compare it with the measured tempered hardness.

Theoretical lines for 0.70% C:

\begin{aligned} \mathrm{HRC_{99.9}} &= 35 + 50(0.70) = 70 \\ \mathrm{HRC_{90}} &= 30 + 50(0.70) = 65 \\ \mathrm{HRC_{50}} &= 23 + 50(0.70) = 58 \end{aligned}

Between the 50 and 90% lines, \mathrm{HRC} = 58 + 0.175(M - 50); between 90 and 99.9%, \mathrm{HRC} = 65 + 0.505(M - 90).

Answer: austenitising at 1050^\circ\mathrm{C} agrees better: its deviation is smaller at every tempering temperature, most clearly at the secondary peak, where the RA has transformed.

Reasons for the deviation:

  1. Relation beyond its range. The lines are linear only to about 0.6% C; the graph levels at about 65, 60 and 53 HRC, so at 0.70% C the equations overestimate by about 5 HRC.
  2. Tempering is not in the relation. It describes as-quenched martensite; \varepsilon-carbide precipitation and loss of tetragonality (to 250^\circ\mathrm{C}), then cementite (250 to 350^\circ\mathrm{C}), soften it, hence the minimum near 350^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  3. Retained austenite is soft and carbon-rich, so the martensite holds less than 0.70% C.
  4. Secondary hardening at about 500^\circ\mathrm{C}: RA becomes fresh martensite on cooling and fine alloy carbides precipitate. A plain 1070 cannot do this; the curves belong to an alloyed tool steel. Real 1070 is hardened from about 800^\circ\mathrm{C} (A_3 \approx 750^\circ\mathrm{C}); 1020 to 1050^\circ\mathrm{C} would coarsen its grain.
  5. Why 1050 fits better: more carbon and alloy dissolve, giving harder martensite and more secondary hardening, although the extra RA (25 against 20%) lowers the low-temperature hardness.
  6. Above about 550^\circ\mathrm{C} carbides coarsen and hardness falls steeply, which the relation cannot predict.

4a.html:
Partly agree. With conventional strengthening, higher strength does lower deep drawability, but the right strengthening mechanism separates the two.

Deep drawability is judged by the mean plastic strain ratio

\bar{r} = \frac{r_0 + 2r_{45} + r_{90}}{4}, \qquad r = \frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{width}}}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{thickness}}}

A high \bar r (about 2) means the sheet flows in its plane instead of thinning. It needs clean ferrite with \{111\} planes parallel to the sheet, low yield strength and high n.

Why strength usually limits it (agree):

  • C and N sit in the octahedral sites of BCC ferrite (face centres, edge midpoints). The hole is only 0.154R (about 0.019 nm) against a C radius of 0.077 nm, so the cell is strained tetragonally and dislocations are pinned: yield point, Luders bands, strain ageing.
  • Dissolved C and N suppress the \{111\} annealing texture, so \bar r falls to about 1.0 to 1.2.
  • Pearlite and precipitates cut elongation and n.

Why it need not (disagree):

  • IF steel: C and N below about 30 ppm, fixed by Ti or Nb; strong \{111\} texture, \bar r \approx 2.
  • P-added IF steel: P substitutes for Fe on lattice sites, a small symmetric distortion that strengthens ferrite (0.17% P adds about 62 MPa) without pinning dislocations or spoiling the texture.
  • Bake-hardening, DP and TRIP sheet are soft when pressed and strengthen afterwards.

Conclusion: true for interstitial and second-phase strengthening, false for substitutional strengthening of interstitial-free ferrite.

4b.html:
Practical impacts

(a) High DBTT. Plain carbon steel (coarse ferrite-pearlite, with P and N) turns from ductile to cleavage fracture near or even above room temperature. It then fails suddenly, below the yield stress and without warning, under impact, in cold weather, at notches and in thick welded joints: ship hulls, bridges, tanks, pipelines, pressure vessels and rails. It cannot be used for low-temperature service (LPG and LNG tanks, offshore structures), and impact-tested grades are needed even for ordinary structures.

(b) Poor hardenability. The pearlite nose of plain carbon steel lies at about 1 s, so only the surface of a large section cools faster than the critical rate. On the Jominy bar 1040 falls below 30 HRC within about 10 mm of the quenched end (slide 22). Large shafts, axles and gears are left with a soft ferrite-pearlite core, low core strength and fatigue limit, and uneven properties. The drastic water or brine quench used to compensate causes distortion and quench cracks.

Alloying against high DBTT

  • Ni (1 to 3.5%, 9% for LNG at -196^\circ\mathrm{C}): non-carbide-forming, strengthens ferrite without loss of ductility and lowers the DBTT; only 0.3% Ni shifts the Charpy curve about 40^\circ\mathrm{C} lower (book Fig. 1.81).
  • Mn (0.8 to 1.5%, Mn/S of at least 8): forms MnS instead of FeS and free S at grain boundaries, and refines ferrite and pearlite; the transition falls from about 120^\circ\mathrm{C} at 0% Mn to about -30^\circ\mathrm{C} at 2% Mn (slide 46).
  • Grain refiners Al, Nb, V, Ti (0.02 to 0.1%): finer grains raise yield strength and lower the DBTT together. Keep C, P and N low; 0.2 to 0.5% Mo prevents temper embrittlement.

Alloying against poor hardenability Dissolved Mn, Mo, Cr (and Ni, B) must redistribute before ferrite or pearlite can form, and substitutional atoms diffuse slowly, so the TTT nose moves to longer times and the critical cooling rate falls. The core of a thick section then cools past the nose even in oil, giving martensite with less distortion and cracking. Grossmann factors per wt%: Mn 1 + 3.33\,\%\mathrm{Mn}, Mo 1 + 3.0\,\%\mathrm{Mo}, Cr 1 + 2.16\,\%\mathrm{Cr}; 0.0015 to 0.003% B is very effective in low-C steel.

The best answer to both limits is Ni-Cr-Mo steel: 4340 (1.85Ni-0.8Cr-0.25Mo) stays near 50 HRC 50 mm from the Jominy end and is tough after tempering.

5a.html:
Why it needs a process-line review. Carburising at 950^\circ\mathrm{C} plus a quench distorts the part: long high-temperature hold (sagging, grain growth), austenite-to-martensite volume increase and a steep quench gradient. Straightening and grinding then waste energy and material and remove case: not sustainable.

Why nitriding fixes the dimensions. It runs at about 500 to 570^\circ\mathrm{C} in the ferrite field: no phase change, no quench, only slight predictable growth. Parts can be finish-machined first.

The corrosion problem and the solution. Plain carbon steel has no Al, Cr, V or Mo nitride formers, so nitriding gives a thin, moderate case, and the porous nitrided surface corrodes. Use:

  1. Ferritic nitrocarburising (gas or plasma, about 570^\circ\mathrm{C}): a compound (white) layer of \varepsilon-\mathrm{Fe_{2-3}(C,N)} and \gamma^{\prime}-\mathrm{Fe_4N}, about 700 to 900 HV (slide 4), over a diffusion zone for fatigue.
  2. Post-oxidation: about 1 µm of black \mathrm{Fe_3O_4} that fills the compound-layer pores and passivates. On the nitride layer its Pilling-Bedworth ratio is about 1.7 to 1.8 (protective), against 2.10 on bare ferrite, where it spalls.
  3. Gas or plasma rather than toxic cyanide salt.

Proposal: nitrocarburising + post-oxidation if the loads suit a thin case; otherwise keep carburising but cut distortion (lower temperature, press or gas quench).

Proposes nitrocarburising: \varepsilon and \gamma^{\prime} compound layer for wear over a diffusion zone for fatigue
Proposes post-oxidation: about 1 µm \mathrm{Fe_3O_4} sealing pores and passivating; protective on the nitride layer (R_{PB} about 1.7 to 1.8 against 2.10 on ferrite)

5b.html:
Diagnosis. W-grade steel is plain high-carbon steel (0.6 to 1.3% C) with low hardenability, so it must be water quenched, and cracking is its main problem (slide 8). Fatigue cracks start at surface defects and inclusions, and these come from the process: oxide and sulfide inclusions and segregation in air-melted steel, quench micro-cracks and residual surface tension, a decarburised skin, grinding burns and coarse carbide networks.

Process modifications (same composition):

  1. Cleaner steel: ladle refining with argon stirring (VAD) and electroslag remelting (ESR). The slag removes sulfur and inclusions, and controlled solidification reduces segregation. From slide 15, the fatigue strength at 10^7 cycles rises from about 400 MPa (air melted) to about 600 MPa (ESR).
  2. Preparatory treatment: large forging reduction, normalising to dissolve grain-boundary carbides, then spheroidise annealing for fine, uniform globular carbides.
  3. Controlled hardening: austenitise at about 760 to 800^\circ\mathrm{C} (fine grain) in a salt bath or protective atmosphere (no decarburisation), quench in agitated brine, temper immediately at about 175 to 200^\circ\mathrm{C}, and stress relieve after machining.
  4. Surface: fine grinding without burns, polishing, and shot peening, which leaves compressive surface stress and raises fatigue strength (book p 246).

ESR-quality steel, carefully hardened and shot peened, gives a much longer fatigue life in the same grade.

Proposes secondary refining and ESR (or VAR): less sulfur, fewer inclusions, less segregation; fatigue strength about 400 to 600 MPa at 10^7 cycles
Forging reduction with normalising and spheroidise annealing for fine, uniform globular carbides
Controlled hardening: correct austenitising temperature, salt bath or protective atmosphere, agitated brine, immediate tempering, stress relief
Surface finishing: burn-free grinding, polishing and shot peening for compressive residual stress

5c.html:
Why the line needs review. A martensitic stainless steel (410, 420) used without heat treatment is in the annealed state: ferrite plus Cr carbides, about 160 HB, YS 300 MPa, UTS 500 MPa. It cannot hold an edge or resist wear and seat erosion, and much of its Cr is locked in carbides, so its corrosion resistance, already the lowest of the stainless families, falls further. Hardening it needs austenitising, quenching and tempering (avoiding 420 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C}), which brings distortion, cracking and decarburisation risk.

Proposed solution: 17-4 PH (AISI 630). Low C (at most 0.07%), 16% Cr, 4% Ni, 4% Cu, Nb.

  1. Solution anneal at about 1040^\circ\mathrm{C} (Condition A): low-C martensite with no retained austenite, machinable.
  2. Machine valves and instruments to final size.
  3. Age at 480 to 620^\circ\mathrm{C}: fine Cu precipitates. Tensile strength about 1310 MPa (YS about 1170 MPa) after 1 h at 480^\circ\mathrm{C} (instruments), about 930 MPa with better toughness after 4 h at 620^\circ\mathrm{C} (valves).

There is no quench after machining, so distortion is small; Cr stays in solution, so corrosion resistance is better.
pts: Identifies the problem: unhardened martensitic stainless is soft annealed ferrite plus carbides (about 160 HB), poor wear and edge retention
Corrosion is low because Cr is tied up in carbides; hardening it adds distortion and cracking risk and the 420 to 600 degrees C tempering limit
Proposes a PH grade (17-4 PH or 15-5 PH) with its low-C, Cr-Ni-Cu composition
Solution anneal at about 1040 degrees C, machine, then age at 480 to 620 degrees C to precipitate Cu
Benefits with values: strength about 1310 MPa (480 degrees C) or 930 MPa (620 degrees C), little distortion, better toughness and corrosion resistance

5d.html:
Why it needs review. Eutectic carbide (massive cementite) makes ductile-iron pipe brittle, hard and difficult to machine, and the pipe may crack during fettling and handling (slide 5). It then fails its ductility, impact and pressure tests. Centrifugally cast pipe solidifies fast against a water-cooled metal mould, and Mg treatment with weak inoculation also promotes carbide. For pipe, carbide removal is therefore a regular production step (book p 297), not an accident.

Solution: graphitising anneal (slides 7, 10).

  1. Heat to 900 to 925^\circ\mathrm{C}, in the austenite + graphite field, and hold for at least 2 h (longer for thick walls). The carbide dissolves, \mathrm{Fe_3C} \rightarrow 3\mathrm{Fe}(\gamma) + \mathrm{C}, and the carbon diffuses through the austenite onto the existing nodules. The decomposition rate doubles for every 55^\circ\mathrm{C} rise (slide 7).
  2. Cool to set the matrix. For a ferritic pipe (grades 60-45-12, 60-40-18), furnace cool at 95^\circ\mathrm{C}/h to 700^\circ\mathrm{C}, then at 55^\circ\mathrm{C}/h to 345^\circ\mathrm{C}, and air cool. Where fast cooling is practical, as in a continuous pipe oven, use the two-stage cycle: fast cool to 675 to 700^\circ\mathrm{C}, hold at 730^\circ\mathrm{C} for 2 h per inch, air cool. Air cooling from the anneal (normalising) gives a stronger pearlitic pipe instead.
  3. Check by metallography (no carbide, nodules in ferrite) and hardness.

Better inoculation and lower Cr and Mn cut the carbide at source and shorten the anneal.
pts: Explains why the carbides need action: brittle, hard, poor machinability, cracking in fettling, failed tests
Gives the cause: fast freezing in a water-cooled metal mould, Mg treatment, weak inoculation; carbide removal is routine for pipe

Controlled cooling for ferrite: 95^\circ\mathrm{C}/h to 700^\circ\mathrm{C}, then 55^\circ\mathrm{C}/h to 345^\circ\mathrm{C}, air cool; or the two-stage cycle with the 730^\circ\mathrm{C} hold

6a.html:
Ranking, most to least important for microstructural change in cast iron: Si > S > Mn > Mo > P.

The criterion is how strongly, at its usual level, the element shifts the graphite-cementite balance (grey, mottled or white iron), the graphite shape and the matrix (ferrite or pearlite).

  1. Si (1 to 3%), first. The main graphitiser. It destabilises cementite and lowers the carbon solubility, so together with C it decides grey or white iron through the carbon equivalent, \mathrm{CE} = \%\mathrm{C} + (\%\mathrm{Si} + \%\mathrm{P})/3. It also promotes a ferritic matrix and raises the eutectoid temperature. It is present in the largest amount, and every grade is set by C and Si.
  2. S (0.01 to 0.15%), second. Very strong per unit amount. As FeS it stabilises cementite and gives chilled or mottled iron. It also controls graphite shape: S must be below about 0.02% before Mg treatment for nodular graphite, otherwise flakes form. The S level also fixes how much Mn is free.
  3. Mn (0.1 to 1.2%), third. Its effect depends on S. Mn first forms MnS, \%\mathrm{Mn} = 1.7\,\%\mathrm{S}, which removes the carbide-forming FeS. Only the excess resists graphitisation and stabilises pearlite: 1.7\,\%\mathrm{S} + 0.15 gives maximum ferrite, 3\,\%\mathrm{S} + 0.35 a pearlitic matrix. A strong matrix control, but secondary to S.
  4. Mo (deliberate addition, up to about 1%), fourth. A mild pearlite promoter that refines pearlite and raises hardenability (heavy sections, ADI), and forms intercellular carbides in heavy sections. Little effect on graphite.
  5. P (0.02 to 0.3%), last. Practically no effect on the graphite-cementite ratio or the matrix. It only forms steadite, a low-melting (about 950^\circ\mathrm{C}) phosphide eutectic at cell boundaries. Its importance lies in properties: shrinkage porosity, cold shortness, low ductility.

Conclusion: Si, and S with Mn, decide what kind of cast iron forms; Mo and P only modify it.
pts: Gives a clear ranking and states the criterion (graphite against cementite, graphite shape, matrix)
Ranks Si first: main graphitiser, sets grey or white iron through CE, promotes ferrite, present in the largest amount
Justifies S: FeS stabilises cementite (chill, mottle); S below about 0.02% needed for nodular graphite; strong per unit amount
Justifies Mn: first ties up S as MnS (Mn = 1.7S), excess promotes pearlite; gives the 1.7S + 0.15 and 3S + 0.35 rules
Justifies Mo: mild pearlite promoter, hardenability, intercellular carbides in heavy sections
Justifies P last: no effect on graphite-cementite ratio, forms steadite; affects properties rather than structure
Concludes and defends the order, noting that S and Mn act as a pair

6b.html:
AISI 316 (at most 0.08% C, 16 to 18% Cr, 10 to 14% Ni, 2 to 3% Mo) is used after solution annealing. It recrystallises cold-worked grains, reverts strain-induced martensite, relieves stress and restores ductility and corrosion resistance.

Annealing cycle

  1. Prepare and load: degrease (no carbon or sulphur pickup); space and support the parts, since thermal expansion is about 50% above carbon steel.
  2. Heat steadily: conductivity is only a fifth of iron's, so thick sections need time to equalise.
  3. Soak at 1040 to 1120^\circ\mathrm{C} (typically about 1065^\circ\mathrm{C}), about 1 h per 25 mm.
  4. Cool fast: water quench thick sections, rapid air or gas cool for sheet, so that 900 to 450^\circ\mathrm{C} is crossed in minutes. Do not over-quench thin parts (distortion).
  5. Atmosphere: bright anneal in dry \mathrm{H_2} or cracked \mathrm{NH_3} (dew point below -50^\circ\mathrm{C}), or anneal in air and pickle.
  6. If stress relief is needed later, use 425 to 550^\circ\mathrm{C}, where \mathrm{M_{23}C_6} forms very slowly.

Role of precipitates in the temperature choice

  • Lower limit from \mathrm{M_{23}C_6}: Cr-rich carbides (M = Cr, Fe, Mo) precipitate at grain boundaries at 450 to 900^\circ\mathrm{C} and cause sensitisation. Annealing must be above 900^\circ\mathrm{C}, and dissolution is slow.
  • Mo raises the minimum: Mo stabilises the carbides and forms sigma, chi and Laves phases (about 600 to 900^\circ\mathrm{C}). So 316 needs at least 1040^\circ\mathrm{C}, against 1010^\circ\mathrm{C} for 304.
  • Upper limit 1120^\circ\mathrm{C}: once the boundary-pinning particles dissolve, grains coarsen; patchy dissolution gives abnormal grain growth (secondary recrystallisation).
  • Cooling rate: fast enough that carbides and intermetallics cannot re-precipitate on the way down.

Protective (bright) atmosphere or pickling; stress relief only at 425 to 550 degrees C
\mathrm{M_{23}C_6} forms at 450 to 900 degrees C and causes sensitisation, so the anneal must exceed 900 degrees C and dissolve it fully
Mo stabilises carbides and forms sigma, chi and Laves, so 316 needs at least 1040 degrees C (304 only 1010 degrees C)
Upper limit 1120 degrees C: dissolved particles no longer pin boundaries, so grain growth and abnormal grain growth set in

7a.html:
Plot (slide 27): hardness against tempering temperature, or the tempering parameter T(c + \log t), falls into four classes:

ClassSteelsCurve
1carbon and low alloy (W, O)highest start, falls steadily: \mathrm{Fe_3C} precipitates and coarsens
2medium to high alloy cold work (A2, D2)plateau (D2 holds to about 425^\circ\mathrm{C}), then drops: Cr retards carbide coarsening
3high-alloy high-speed (M2, T1)slight dip, secondary peak near 550^\circ\mathrm{C} that can exceed the as-quenched value, steep fall
4medium to high alloy hot work (H13)lowest start (about 0.4% C), flat, small hump near 550^\circ\mathrm{C}

Reasoning: carbide content sets the schedule

  1. Carbide type. Cementite coarsens at low temperature, so class 1 is tempered low, about 150 to 200^\circ\mathrm{C} (O series below 200^\circ\mathrm{C}, slide 9); with little retained austenite, the standard double temper (slide 29) is enough. Stable alloy carbides of V, Mo, W and Cr resist softening, so classes 2 to 4 can be tempered at 500 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  2. Carbide dissolved on austenitising. High-speed steels carry up to 20 vol% carbide and are hardened near the solidus. The dissolved C and alloy lower M_s and leave 20 to 30% retained austenite, which transforms only on cooling from high-temperature tempering, into fresh martensite that itself needs tempering. Hence two or three tempers, each cooled to room temperature (slide 29).
  3. Position of the secondary peak. Class 3: at or just above the peak, 540 to 570^\circ\mathrm{C}, three times, for maximum hardness and red hardness. Class 4 (up to 5 vol% carbide): above the peak, about 550 to 650^\circ\mathrm{C}, twice, for toughness and above the service temperature. Class 2 (up to 25 vol% in 12% Cr ledeburitic steel): low, about 200^\circ\mathrm{C}, for maximum hardness, or near its small peak (500 to 540^\circ\mathrm{C}, twice) to transform retained austenite for dimensional stability.
  4. Dimensional change. Alloy-carbide precipitation and retained-austenite transformation change the volume (tempering stages 3 to 5), so large or complex tools and gauges get a third temper.

7b.html:
Why the carbon equivalent is high

The carbon equivalent adds each alloying element weighted by its effect on hardenability and crack sensitivity (course book p 131):

CE = \%\mathrm{C} + \frac{\%\mathrm{Mn}}{5} + \frac{\%\mathrm{Cr}}{4} + \frac{\%\mathrm{Mo}}{3} + \frac{\%\mathrm{Ni}}{10} + \frac{\%\mathrm{V}}{5} + \frac{\%\mathrm{Si} - 0.5}{5} + \frac{\%\mathrm{W}}{10}

High-speed steels combine high carbon (0.7 to 1.3%) with 15 to 25% of strong carbide formers (W, Mo, Cr, V, often Co). For M2 (0.85C-4Cr-5Mo-6W-2V, about 0.3% Mn and Si):

CE \approx 0.85 + 0.06 + 1.00 + 1.67 + 0.40 - 0.04 + 0.60 \approx 4.5

This is far above 0.7, beyond which steel is very crack sensitive. The alloy also lowers thermal conductivity and makes the steel air hardening from about 1200^\circ\mathrm{C}, so steep gradients act on brittle martensite plus carbides. HSS are therefore preheated in two stages, 500 to 550^\circ\mathrm{C} and 850^\circ\mathrm{C} (slide 30). The alloy also needs its own carbon: \%\mathrm{C} \geq (\%\mathrm{W} + 1.9\,\%\mathrm{Mo} + 6.3\,\%\mathrm{V})/30 + 0.1 (slide 31; book p 261).

Softening and hardening during tempering (slide 28)

Three effects overlap:

  1. Softening of martensite (falls throughout): \varepsilon-carbide, then cementite, precipitate; carbon leaves the martensite, tetragonality is lost and dislocations recover. It dominates up to about 350^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  2. Transformation of retained austenite (from about 450 to 500^\circ\mathrm{C}): the 20 to 30% soft retained austenite loses C and alloy to carbides, its M_s rises, and on cooling it becomes fresh hard martensite.
  3. Alloy-carbide precipitation (above about 500^\circ\mathrm{C}): W, Mo and V can now diffuse and form ultrafine coherent \mathrm{M_2C} (\mathrm{Mo_2C}, \mathrm{W_2C}) and MC (VC) that pin dislocations.

Their sum dips to a minimum near 350 to 450^\circ\mathrm{C} and rises to a secondary peak at about 500 to 570^\circ\mathrm{C}, which can exceed the as-quenched hardness (book Fig 4.31: about 63.5 HRC quenched, 61 HRC at 300^\circ\mathrm{C}, 64.5 HRC near 530^\circ\mathrm{C}). Above about 600^\circ\mathrm{C} the carbides coarsen and hardness falls steeply (46 HRC by 800^\circ\mathrm{C}). This peak is the red hardness; the fresh martensite needs further tempers, so HSS are tempered two or three times at 540 to 570^\circ\mathrm{C}.

8a.html:
Eddy currents from a water-cooled copper coil heat only the surface layer, which is then spray-quenched to martensite over a tough core. For symmetrical parts:

1. Steel and prior structure. At least 0.3% C, normally 0.4 to 0.5% C (AISI 1045; 4140 for a stronger core), quenched and tempered or normalised so fine carbides dissolve in seconds. Case hardness 35 + 50(0.45) \approx 57 HRC.

2. Inductor and coupling. Coil shaped to the part, uniform gap 1 to 3 mm: encircling coil for shafts, axles, spindles and cam lobes (single-shot, or scanning for long parts); spinning gear in an encircling coil (small module) or a tooth-gap inductor (large gears). Rotate the part; holes, slots and sharp edges concentrate current and crack.

3. Frequency (depth control).

\delta = 5.03\sqrt{\frac{\rho}{\mu f}}\ \mathrm{cm}

For hot steel (\rho \approx 115\ \mu\Omega\,\mathrm{cm}, \mu = 1 above 770^\circ\mathrm{C}): \delta \approx 0.85 mm at 400 kHz, 1.7 mm at 100 kHz, 5.4 mm at 10 kHz, 9.8 mm at 3 kHz. Use 100 to 450 kHz for cases near 1 mm, about 10 kHz for 2 to 3 mm, 1 to 3 kHz for deep cases. Gears: dual frequency (low to heat the roots, high for the tips) gives a contour case.

4. Temperature, power and time. About 900 to 1000^\circ\mathrm{C}, well above furnace practice (book p 132: 950 to 1000^\circ\mathrm{C} for a steel furnace-hardened at 830 to 850^\circ\mathrm{C}): rapid heating raises Ac3 and leaves little time for carbide solution. Power density about 1 to 2 kW/cm² for 1 to 10 s, or a fixed scan speed. Generator size:

P = P_1 + P_2 + P_3 + P_4 \approx \frac{3 \times 4.186\,MC\,\Delta T}{t}

(about 37 kW for a 1.5 mm case on a 25 mm by 50 mm bar in 2 s).

5. Quench. Integral spray ring, quench delay under about 1 s, water or 5 to 15% polymer (alloy steels), part rotating until below M_f.

6. Temper at 150 to 200^\circ\mathrm{C} for about 1 h.

7. Control. Energy monitor and pyrometer; section sample parts for hardness, case depth and cracks.

8b.html:
Choice: gas carburising.

  1. Hardenability. Plain carbon steel needs a fast, prompt quench. A sealed-quench gas furnace quenches directly from the furnace; a pack must be cooled, unpacked and reheated.
  2. Grain size. Plain carbon steels without grain refiners coarsen in long holds. Gas is faster (no box to heat through, continuous carbon supply), so grains grow less.
  3. Carbon control. The CO/CO2 ratio and dew point set the carbon potential: boost, then diffuse to about 0.8 to 0.9% C at the surface. A pack saturates the surface (about 1.2 to 1.3% C), giving a cementite network and retained austenite.
  4. Uniform case, clean parts, mass production. Against it: costly furnace and generator, skilled operators, CO fire and toxic hazards; pack remains for small batches, very large parts and selective carburising.

Reactions. Pack: \mathrm{BaCO_3 \rightarrow BaO + CO_2}, \mathrm{CO_2 + C \rightarrow 2CO}, \mathrm{2CO \rightarrow C_{(\gamma\text{-}Fe)} + CO_2}. Gas: \mathrm{2CO \rightarrow C_{(\gamma\text{-}Fe)} + CO_2}, \mathrm{CH_4 \rightarrow C_{(\gamma\text{-}Fe)} + 2H_2}, \mathrm{CO + H_2 \rightleftharpoons C_{(\gamma\text{-}Fe)} + H_2O}.

Carbon depth calculation (slide 16 data)

Given: C_0 = 0.15\%, C_s = 1.30\%, C_x = 0.30\% at x = 2 mm, 900^\circ\mathrm{C}; D \approx 2.04\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}} (slide 15, 1173 K, averaged over 0.15 to 1.3% C).

Find: the carburising time.

Solution:

\begin{aligned} \frac{C_s - C_x}{C_s - C_0} &= \mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{Dt}}\right) = \frac{1.30 - 0.30}{1.30 - 0.15} = 0.870 \\ \frac{x}{2\sqrt{Dt}} &= 1.069 \\ t &= \frac{x^2}{4D(1.069)^2} = \frac{(0.20\ \mathrm{cm})^2}{4(2.04\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}})(1.143)} = 4.29\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}

Answer: t \approx 11.9 h. Since x \propto \sqrt{t}, a 1 mm case needs about 3 h. The equation assumes a constant C_s, which only a controlled gas atmosphere maintains.

Microstructural changes

  • At 900^\circ\mathrm{C}: ferrite + pearlite becomes austenite, carbon diffuses in, grains grow with time.
  • Slowly cooled (slide 7), surface to core: hypereutectoid (pearlite + grain-boundary cementite), eutectoid (all pearlite), hypoeutectoid (pearlite + rising ferrite), core (ferrite + little pearlite).
  • Quenched and tempered at 150 to 180^\circ\mathrm{C}: case of tempered high-carbon martensite with some retained austenite (about 60 to 64 HRC), grading to lath martensite; core low-carbon lath martensite, or ferrite + bainite in thick plain carbon sections.
